perspective:
Mason’s available information is limited to his own observations, actions, statements, and feelings:

- He reviewed the community center’s financial reports and noticed discrepancies, especially unusually high healthcare expenses that did not match usual spending patterns. He became suspicious and anxious, initially suspecting Martha might be mismanaging funds.
- He spoke with Martha about the report. He told her the numbers did not add up and pointed to the healthcare expense section. He heard Martha say there might have been a misentry and that she would review and correct any errors.
- After reviewing/clarifying with Martha, he came to believe the discrepancies were due to a simple clerical error, not mismanagement. He felt relieved and embarrassed. He apologized to Martha for his initial suspicion; he heard her say it was okay, that errors happen, and that they should double-check entries next time.
- He later believed Martha was competent and that the real problem was the current financial management system. He felt frustrated with the system but empathetic toward Martha. He proposed drafting a new, more robust financial system and heard Martha agree and offer to help.
- He drafted the proposal, felt hopeful it would benefit operations, but was uncertain whether management would approve it. He told Martha he finished the draft; he heard her call it solid, encourage a confident presentation, and agree to help gather data. He planned a detailed presentation.
- After presenting the proposal to management, he believed the presentation went well, felt satisfied but physically/mentally exhausted, and believed he had done everything possible. He told Martha it was now up to management. He heard Martha praise him, suggest taking time off, and offer support. He planned to take a few days off to recharge and reflect, hoping for good news.
- He does not know management’s final decision unless later informed; he only knows the proposal was presented and is pending.
